Small, intrinsic inconsistencies between the absorption profiles of different transitions may also arise if some of the absorbing gas only partially covers the background quasar, or if HE 0515−-4414 is gravitationally lensed, with multiple, as-yet-unresolved sight-lines combining to produce the observed spectrum. Previous attempts to assess these effects in slit-based spectrographs (Kotuš et al., 2017, e.g.) have been hampered by both the long-range and intra-order distortions of the wavelength scale (see Section 1). Clearly, these will both shift different transitions relative to each other depending on where they fall on the CCD mosaic. However, ESPRESSO’s high-accuracy wavelength calibration avoids this. Therefore, ESPRESSO offers an important, alternative check on profile modelling errors to those derived above (Section 4.2.2).

Figure 10 shows the best-fitted velocity shifts between transitions for the right region. Here, Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha was fixed to zero in the fiducial model and a velocity shift was introduced as a free parameter for all fitting regions except that for M​g​i​λ​2852{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852}, i.e. all velocity shifts are measured with respect to this transition. Fig. 10 clearly demonstrates that there are no systematic velocity shifts between transitions: all transitions are consistent with M​g​i​λ​2852{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852} and with each other. The stronger, unsaturated transitions in the right region also provide very precise velocity shift measurements: e.g. the five strong Fe ii lines only have ≈30\approx 30 m s−1\textrm{m\,s}^{-1} uncertainties. Collectively, there is also no evidence for a shift between species: the weighed mean shift for the Fe ii lines is −6±16-6\pm 16 m s−1\textrm{m\,s}^{-1} from the M​g​i​λ​2852{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852} line. Taken together, the results in Fig. 10 support the assumptions of the MM method and indicate that our profile fitting approach is robust.

4.3.6 Isotopic abundance variations

Most of the transitions fitted in the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber have isotopic structures whose components span velocity ranges of ≈\approx0.4 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} for Fe ii to ≈\approx0.5–1 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} for the Mg i/ii transitions. As explained in Section 3.3, we assume the terrestrial isotopic abundances for each element in our analysis. However, if the abundances are different in the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber, we will spuriously infer shifts between different transitions and, therefore, in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha. This is a well-recognised problem (Murphy et al., 2001b; Ashenfelter et al., 2004a; Ashenfelter et al., 2004b; Levshakov et al., 2005) but, unfortunately, there are currently no strong and reliable constraints on the isotopic abundances in quasar absorbers (Agafonova et al., 2011; Levshakov et al., 2009; Webb et al., 2014; Vangioni & Olive, 2019; Noterdaeme et al., 2018, e.g.). For the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber, the ≈\approx0.5 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}-wide isotopic structure of M​g​i​λ​2852{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852} is particularly important. If, for example, the dominant 24Mg isotope (79% terrestrial abundance) was not present in the absorber and the two heavier isotopes (25,26Mg) were equally abundant, this would cause a ≈\approx6 ppm spurious shift in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha (Fenner et al., 2005, e.g.). Possible isotopic abundance variations are therefore a potentially important systematic effect for our Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha measurements.

The velocity shift results in Fig. 10 demonstrate that large isotopic abundance variations in the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber are very unlikely. The Fe ii lines are shifted by just −6±16-6\pm 16 m s−1\textrm{m\,s}^{-1} relative to the M​g​i​λ​2852{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852} line in the right region (see Section 4.3.5 above). For comparison, the velocity between the M24​g​i​λ​2852{}^{24}{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852} laboratory wavelength and the composite value with terrestrial isotopic abundances is 65 m s−1\textrm{m\,s}^{-1}. So, if the heavier isotopes (25,26Mg) have zero abundance in the absorber, we should see a velocity shift of this order between the Fe ii transitions and M​g​i​λ​2852{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852} (assuming Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha is zero). Similarly, if only the heavier isotopes were present, with equal abundances in the absorber, we would expect to measure a 241 m s−1\textrm{m\,s}^{-1} shift between the Fe ii and M​g​i​λ​2852{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852} lines. Clearly, these extreme isotopic abundance variations are not favoured by the results in Fig. 10. However, a robust estimate of the isotopic abundance of Mg in the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber is not possible with such a simplistic analysis, and we leave this for future work. Nevertheless, given the difference of ≈\approx0.04 in QQ between the Fe ii and M​g​i​λ​2852{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852} transitions (see Fig. 3), the observed shift of −6±16-6\pm 16 m s−1\textrm{m\,s}^{-1} between them corresponds to a systematic error in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha of <<0.7 ppm.

With their high S/N UVES spectrum, Kotuš et al. (2017) were able to strongly constrain the effect of isotopic abundance variations on their measurement of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha in the same zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber. They removed the influence of Mg i and ii transitions on Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha by introducing velocity shift parameters (as we did for several tests in this Section), finding a negligible 0.24 ppm change in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha, with only a marginal increase in the uncertainty. The latter point is due to the availability of the F​e​ii​λ​1608{Fe\textsc{ii}}\,\lambda\textrm{1608} transition in the UVES spectrum: its large negative QQ coefficient offers a high contrast with the other Fe ii transitions which all have large positive QQ values. We cannot perform the same test with our ESPRESSO spectrum because it does not cover the F​e​ii​λ​1608{Fe\textsc{ii}}\,\lambda\textrm{1608} transition (which falls at ≈\approx3460 Å, cf. ESPRESSO’s blue wavelength limit of ≈\approx3800 Å). Nevertheless, the consistency between our Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha measurement, which depends on the Mg isotopic abundances, and Kotuš et al. (2017)’s which does not (see 5.2 below) indicates that the Mg isotopic abundance effect is likely smaller than ≈\approx1 ppm in our measurement, consistent with the more direct estimate above.

We include our systematic error upper limit of <<0.7 ppm in Table 3. As in previous studies (Kotuš et al., 2017; Milaković et al., 2021, e.g.), we do not include this astrophysical effect in the formal systematic error budget for Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha. However, it is possible that the ESPRESSO data presented here, and the existing UVES spectrum, could be analysed together to formally, and more robustly, constrain (or perhaps measure) the 25,26Mg/24Mg abundance ratio directly. This would then provide a more stringent measurement or limit on the effect on Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha in this specific absorber. We defer this to future work.

4.4 Combined result for the entire absorber

Table 3 summarises the fiducial fitting results with the 1σ\sigma statistical and systematic uncertainties for each of the three regions. The Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha values and uncertainties for each region are independent, so straight-forward Gaussian error propagation can be used to compute the weighted mean result for the entire absorber:

Δ​α/α=1.3±1.3stat±0.4sys​ppm,\Delta\alpha/\alpha=1.3\pm 1.3_{\rm stat}\pm 0.4_{\rm sys}\,{\rm ppm}, (2)

with 1σ\sigma statistical and systematic error components. The right region dominates this combined result. In particular, the three main systematic effects (Section 4.2.1–4.2.3) cause similar uncertainties in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha for the right region, and so make similar contributions to the systematic error combined across the regions.

The result in equation (2) is consistent with no change in the fine-structure constant between the absorber at zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 and the current laboratory value. The systematic uncertainty is well below the statistical one, which is remarkable given that the latter is similar to the ensemble precision obtained from previous large samples of absorbers (see Section 4.1 for discussion). This is because ESPRESSO’s accurate LFC wavelength calibration removes the systematic effects that undermine confidence in those large-sample results. Even the more recent results which were corrected for these effects using asteroid and/or solar twin spectra had residual wavelength calibration uncertainties 0.5–3.5 ppm, larger than our total systematic error budget (Evans et al., 2014; Murphy & Cooksey, 2017, e.g.). As explained in Section 4.2, Kotuš et al. (2017) corrected the wavelength scale of their UVES spectrum of HE 0515−-4414 by using the HARPS spectrum of the same quasar. However, this procedure still left a ∼\sim0.6 ppm wavelength calibration uncertainty which dominated their systematic error budget. The recent Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha measurement in the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber by Milaković et al. (2021) used an LFC-calibrated HARPS spectrum to measure Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha, thereby avoiding wavelength calibration uncertainties like our ESPRESSO spectrum. Of course, the lower S/N of the HARPS spectrum (≈\approx58 per km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}, cf. 170 for our ESPRESSO spectrum) limited the precision to 2.4 ppm (see further discussion in Section 5.2 below).

5 Discussion

5.1 No substantial wavelength calibration errors

As noted in Section 1, several of ESPRESSO’s design features should strongly suppress systematic errors in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha measurements – i.e. relative velocity shifts between transitions at different wavelengths. However, even though the wavelength scale in this study was calibrated with the laser frequency comb (LFC), instrumental effects – particularly illumination-dependent PSF variations across the spectrum – may still affect measurements of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha in general (Schmidt et al., 2021). The four tests described in Sections 4.3.1–4.3.4 all probe these possible wavelength calibration errors. The results are summarised in the lower section of Table 3. For the specific case of the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber studied here, the effect on any wavelength calibration errors on Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha is negligible. However, we again emphasise that this may not be true for ESPRESSO studies of other absorbers, particularly those where important transitions fall towards the red edges of echelle orders in the blue arm. We recommend that quasar observations with ESPRESSO be complemented with asteroid or solar twin exposures to check the wavelength scale, especially if the LFC is not operational (Molaro et al., 2008a; Rahmani et al., 2013; Evans et al., 2014; Whitmore & Murphy, 2015, e.g.).

5.2 Comparison with previous measurements in the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber

The previous measurements of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha at zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 towards HE 0515−-4414 are compared to our new value from ESPRESSO in Fig. 11 (blue points). All measurements are consistent with no variation in α\alpha, and are also consistent with our result. The early UVES measurements by Quast et al. (2004), Chand et al. (2006) and Molaro et al. (2008b) (Levshakov et al., 2006, who revised their earlier measurement in) will all be subject to additional systematic errors, to differing degrees, from the long-range wavelength calibration distortions discussed in Section 1 (Rahmani et al., 2013; Whitmore & Murphy, 2015, e.g.). Kotuš et al. (2017) demonstrated this explicitly, finding that these earlier results most likely require corrections by ∼⁣+\sim+2 ppm, similar to their statistical uncertainties. Kotuš et al. corrected for these effects in their Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha measurement by directly comparing their UVES spectra to a (ThAr-calibrated) HARPS spectrum of the same quasar. The HARPS ThAr calibration has no evident long-range distortions (Whitmore & Murphy, 2015). Milaković et al. (2021) performed the first LFC-calibrated measurement of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha with new HARPS observations, with a separate study of wavelength calibration errors demonstrating that they are negligible for that work (Milaković et al., 2020).

Focussing on these three recent, independent results with relatively low wavelength calibration errors, Fig. 11 indicates the formal weighted mean value for the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber towards HE 0515−-4414:

Δ​α/α=−0.62±0.50stat±0.48sys​ppm.\Delta\alpha/\alpha=-0.62\pm 0.50_{\rm stat}\pm 0.48_{\rm sys}\,{\rm ppm}. (3)

Again, this is consistent with no variation in α\alpha. It is also consistent, at 1.6σ\sigma, with the expected value from the α\alpha dipole of King et al. (2012), i.e. 2.2±1.62.2\pm 1.6 ppm. This value derives from the simplest dipole model where Δ​α/α=10.2−1.9+2.2​cos⁡(Θ)\Delta\alpha/\alpha=10.2_{-1.9}^{+2.2}\cos(\Theta) ppm for Θ\Theta the angle between HE 0515−-4414 and the model’s pole (RA=17.4±0.9{\rm RA}=17.4\pm 0.9 h, Dec.=−58±9∘{\rm Dec.}=-58\pm 9^{\circ}). The line of sight towards HE 0515−-4414’s is almost orthogonal to the dipole direction (Θ=78∘\Theta=78^{\circ}), so the model expectation is near zero, i.e. HE 0515−-4414 does not provide a strong test of the dipole model.

We note that the weighted mean in equation (3) is dominated by the Kotuš et al. (2017) measurement from wavelength-corrected UVES spectra. Despite their considerable efforts to estimate the error budget correctly, it remains plausible that their statistical and systematic uncertainties may be underestimated. For example, the model non-uniqueness problem discussed below (Section 5.4) could affect both the statistical uncertainty and contribute a larger systematic error than previously estimated. These problems potentially extend to all measurements, but it is prudent to be cautious when combining results, especially when one dominates. If we exclude that measurement, the weighted mean of Milaković et al. (2021)’s HARPS result and our ESPRESSO measurement is Δ​α/α=0.93±1.14stat±0.33sys​ppm\Delta\alpha/\alpha=0.93\pm 1.14_{\rm stat}\pm 0.33_{\rm sys}\,{\rm ppm}, where the statistical uncertainty is, of course, larger than in equation (3) but the systematic uncertainty is smaller, reflecting the suppression of systematic effects in the two LFC-calibrated measurements.

5.3 Comparison with recent measurements in other absorbers

Figure 11 also compares our result, and the average for the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber [equation (3)], to other recent measurements which had relatively small wavelength calibration uncertainties (orange points). Evans et al. (2014) used asteroid and iodine-cell exposures to correct the wavelength scales of UVES, HIRES and Subaru/HDS spectra of the same quasar. Similarly, Murphy & Cooksey (2017) corrected HDS spectra of two quasars using exposures of solar twins. Using a different approach, Murphy et al. (2016) measured Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha using only the (normally weak) Zn/Cr ii transitions in ‘metal-strong’ absorbers towards 9 quasars. These ions’ transitions have large sensitivity coefficients (QQ) with opposite sign, making them sensitive probes of α\alpha but, most importantly, the transitions have very similar wavelengths, rendering the Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha measurements insensitive to long-range calibration distortions. Combining the 28 results of these studies with the weighted mean for zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 towards HE 0515−-4414 [equation (3)], we obtain

Δ​α/α=−0.51±0.48stat±0.42sys​ppm.\Delta\alpha/\alpha=-0.51\pm 0.48_{\rm stat}\pm 0.42_{\rm sys}\,{\rm ppm}. (4)

This weighted mean result represents the most reliable measurement using quasar absorption lines, and is relatively free of the long-range wavelength calibration errors that affected all previous spectra, including the large samples from HIRES (Webb et al., 2001; Murphy et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2004) and UVES (Webb et al., 2011; King et al., 2012). As with equation (3), the Kotuš et al. (2017) measurement in the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber also dominates equation (4). Excluding that single result yields a weighted mean of Δ​α/α=0.51±0.82stat±0.37sys​ppm\Delta\alpha/\alpha=0.51\pm 0.82_{\rm stat}\pm 0.37_{\rm sys}\,{\rm ppm}, which still represents ppm-level precision. Again, as in Section 5.2, we urge some caution when combining many results together: if uncorrected systematic errors remain, or some measurements have underestimated total uncertainties, these will significantly affect the weighted mean result.

For 27 of the 29 measurements with low wavelength calibration errors in Fig. 11 – those prior to 2021 – Martins & Pinho (2017) and Murphy & Cooksey (2017) have already noted that they do not support the α\alpha dipole model. Ignoring uncertainties in the model itself, those 27 results are inconsistent with it at the ≈\approx4σ\sigma level. However, if the dominant Kotuš et al. (2017) measurement is removed, this falls to ≈\approx2.5σ\sigma (Murphy & Cooksey, 2017). Our new ESPRESSO measurement, and Milaković et al. (2021)’s HARPS measurement, do not appreciably alter this conclusion, given the near orthogonal directions to HE 0515−-4414 and the dipole.

5.4 Velocity structure

As shown in Table 2, our fitting approach requires a large number of velocity components to fit all the statistical structure of the ESPRESSO spectrum: 48 in the right region of the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber, compared to 49 in Kotuš et al. (2017)’s fit to their UVES spectrum, and 26 for Milaković et al. (2021)’s HARPS spectrum. We mentioned in Section 3.5 that the former two are likely similar because the ESPRESSO and UVES spectra have similar S/N per km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} and because the fitting approach was very similar. The HARPS spectrum’s S/N per km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} is much lower than ESPRESSO’s (≈\approx58 vs. ≈\approx170), so we should expect fewer components to be fitted by Milaković et al. (2021). However, they also used a very different fitting approach: an automated algorithm for determining the velocity structure with vpfit, called ai-vpfit (Lee et al., 2021a), and both turbulent and thermal broadening for each component’s bb parameter (‘compound’ broadening). As a simple illustration, Fig. 12 shows the compound model of Milaković et al. (2021) for part of their region I (corresponding to part of our left region), with χ2\chi^{2} minimised using vpfit on our ESPRESSO spectrum. It is immediately clear that this fit does not adequately account for the statistical structure in the data: e.g. the composite residual spectrum shows several systematic excursions, correlated over many pixels, particularly around the strongest absorption at −540-540 to −525-525 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}, but at other velocities as well. This clearly demonstrates that the larger S/N per km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} of the ESPRESSO spectrum drives the need for a more complex fit; differences in the fitting approach cannot fully explain this.

Lee et al. (2021b) explored how the ai-vpfit approach produced different velocity structures from different starting points of the algorithm and different broadening model assumptions, and how Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha varied between these models. A similar ‘non-uniqueness’ problem arises for the more interactive, human-guided approach we have employed: different people will choose to introduce new components at different velocities, with different initial parameters, while building up a complex fit, and so produce somewhat different velocity structures for the same dataset. We have attempted to ensure our measurement is robust to this effect by thoroughly exploring alternative velocity structures and incorporating their variance in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha into our error budget – see Section 4.2.2. However, we limited that search to adding or subtracting one component from our fiducial model, as the sheer number of other possibilities is not possible to explore in this way. Lee et al. (2021b) find that turbulent-only models within ai-vpfit produce a larger variety of fits, with a larger range of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha values than the compound broadening approach. While this is certainly a concern, it is important to recognise that this is unlikely to apply simplistically outside ai-vpfit itself. Our turbulent-only fitting approach maximises the number of components using χν2\chi^{2}_{\nu} as the information criterion, while the addition of new components – where in the profile they are added, and with what initial parameters – is judged by the human user. Importantly, that judgement seeks to avoid leaving inconsistencies in the model between different ions and/or transitions. Currently, ai-vpfit appears to solve such potential inconsistencies, at least sometimes, by adding blending components (i.e. from an unidentified species in an unidentified absorber) in some fitting regions; these random blends differ when the algorithm is started with different random seeds – see figures A1–A3 of Lee et al. (2021b) which cover the same fitting range as Fig. 12. A full ai-vpfit analysis of our ESPRESSO spectrum would be very welcome: we make our ESPRESSO spectrum publicly available in Murphy et al. (2021) online for others to analyse, or we will undertake this if ai-vpfit becomes available.

6 Conclusions

In this work we have made the first precise measurement of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha with the new ESPRESSO spectrograph on the VLT. HE 0515−-4414 was observed for 16.1 h to achieve a very high S/N (≈\approx105 per 0.4 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} pixel at 6000 Å) at resolving power R≈145000R\approx 145000, with the wavelength scale of all 17 exposures calibrated using the laser frequency comb (LFC). The entire analysis procedure was developed using a blinded version of the spectrum to avoid human biases; once the blinding was removed, the analysis was re-run without alteration or human interaction. The high RR and S/N revealed that the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorption system was more complex than previous studies found: strong constraints on the relative optical depths of two different Mg i lines confirmed the presence of very narrow velocity components (b<0.5b<0.5 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}) in the strongest absorption feature (Section 3.5). A total of 129 velocity components were required to fit the ≈\approx720 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}-wide absorption profile, with the strongest Mg i and Fe ii transitions providing the main constraints on Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha.

Our new measurement at zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 from the ESPRESSO spectrum is

Δ​α/α=1.3±1.3stat±0.4sys​ppm,\Delta\alpha/\alpha=1.3\pm 1.3_{\rm stat}\pm 0.4_{\rm sys}\,{\rm ppm}\,, (5)

consistent with no cosmological variation in the fine-structure constant. The total error is similar to the ensemble precision of the previous, large samples of absorbers from Keck/HIRES and VLT/UVES that indicated variations at the ≈\approx5 ppm level (Webb et al., 2001; Murphy et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2004; Webb et al., 2011; King et al., 2012), which likely arose from long-range distortions in the wavelength scale (Rahmani et al., 2013; Whitmore & Murphy, 2015, e.g.). Our measurement is free from those systematic errors due to the specific design features of ESPRESSO to suppress them (e.g. octagonal fibre feed, stable vacuum environment, and LFC calibration). However, we emphasise that wavelength calibration errors are still possible with ESPRESSO, and future studies of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha should specifically test for them, especially when important transitions fall in the blue arm (Section 5.1). The main systematic uncertainties in our measurement arise from ambiguities in fitting the absorption profile, effects from redispersion of the spectra, and convergence of the fitting procedure (Section 4.2).

HE 0515−-4414 is very bright (Gaia G=14.9G=14.9 mag), which has enabled many previous measurements of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha in the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber. Our new Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha measurement in equation (5) is consistent with the two most recent of those from two different spectrographs: the first LFC-calibrated measurement, from HARPS (Milaković et al., 2021, Δ​α/α=−0.3±2.4\Delta\alpha/\alpha=-0.3\pm 2.4 ppm), and the most precise measurement in a single absorber, from a very high S/N UVES spectrum (Kotuš et al., 2017, Δ​α/α=−1.4±0.6stat±0.6sys\Delta\alpha/\alpha=-1.4\pm 0.6_{\rm stat}\pm 0.6_{\rm sys} ppm). Both are relatively free from wavelength calibration uncertainties (see Section 5.2) and can be combined with our ESPRESSO measurement – see[equation (3)]:

Δ​α/α=−0.6±0.5stat±0.5sys​ppm.\Delta\alpha/\alpha=-0.6\pm 0.5_{\rm stat}\pm 0.5_{\rm sys}\,{\rm ppm}.

A sample of 26 other measurements with HIRES, UVES and Subaru/HDS which have been corrected for, or are insensitive to, long-range wavelength distortions are also consistent with our new measurement and have a similar overall precision: Δ​α/α=0.4±1.3stat±0.7sys\Delta\alpha/\alpha=0.4\pm 1.3_{\rm stat}\pm 0.7_{\rm sys} ppm (Evans et al., 2014; Murphy et al., 2016; Murphy & Cooksey, 2017). Combining the 29 independent, low-wavelength calibration error measurements of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha at zabs=0.6z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=0.6–2.4 above yields a weighted mean [equation (4)]:

Δ​α/α=−0.5±0.5stat±0.4sys​ppm.\Delta\alpha/\alpha=-0.5\pm 0.5_{\rm stat}\pm 0.4_{\rm sys}\,{\rm ppm}\,.

Figure 11 summarises these comparisons with previous measurements.

ESPRESSO promises to provide a larger sample of well-calibrated, high quality quasar absorption spectra for measuring Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha through the instrument consortium’s Guaranteed Time Observations and open, competitive observing time. One important, outstanding problem in improving quasar absorption measurements of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha is the lack of observational constraints on how the isotopic abundances in the absorbers differ from the terrestrial values. The overall velocity shifts between M​g​i​λ​2852{Mg\textsc{i}}\,\lambda\textrm{2852} and the strong Fe ii lines in our ESPRESSO spectrum limit the effect on our measurement of Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha to <<0.7 ppm (Section 4.3.6). It may be possible to directly measure the Mg isotopic abundance ratio in this absorber with our spectrum, given ESPRESSO’s excellent wavelength calibration accuracy and, in principle at least, detailed map of the instrumental line-shape function provided by the LFC and Fabry–Pérot calibration exposures. However, given its complex absorption profile, a robust isotopic ratio estimate in the zabs=1.1508z_{\text{\scriptsize abs}}=1.1508 absorber will likely require an even more extensive exploration of alternative velocity structures than we have performed here.

Appendix A Alternative profile models

Here we detail the alternative models used to derive an estimate of the systematic errors from profile model non-uniqueness in Section 4.2.2. Table 4 identifies the velocity at which components were removed from, or added to the fiducial models for the right, central and left regions plotted in Figs. 4, 8 and 9 respectively. In general, we focused on components in the spectral features that most strongly influence Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha. We also investigated other features where two components were fitted close to each other – we removed one of them to assess whether it was really statistically required. The stability, or otherwise, of each model is noted in the table. Note that Table 4 does not show all models attempted: many models were initially investigated which, upon preliminary analysis, were either highly unstable or produced substantially larger χ2\chi^{2} per degree of freedom (χν2\chi^{2}_{\nu}) than the fiducial model and/or large deviations in the composite residual spectra; these were discarded without further consideration.

For the remaining models, Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha was measured in the same way as for the fiducial model (Section 3.3), first using the blinded spectrum and again after unblinding (see Section 3.4). Initially, Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha was fixed at the fiducial value while the alternative model was constructed and refined by minimising χ2\chi^{2} in vpfit. Then vpfit was re-run with Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha as a free parameter. Table 4 shows how Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha deviates from the fiducial value for the region, and the increase in χ2\chi^{2} and the Akaike information criterion, corrected for finite sample sizes, AICC, as a result. Note that some stable alternative models have a lower AICC than the fiducial model. At first, it may seem that one of these models was, therefore, more appropriate to adopt as fiducial. However, this is not correct for two reasons: (i) the fiducial model was selected while the analysis was blinded, so the χν2\chi^{2}_{\nu} and AICC values were based on the blinded spectrum, while those in Table 4 are from the final, unblinded analysis; and (ii) we used χν2\chi^{2}_{\nu} as a simpler information criterion for deciding which model should be the fiducial one, while AICC is perhaps more justified for comparing very similar models as we do in this systematic error analysis.

The most important aspects of the alternative models are discussed below for each region.

A.1 Right region

The spectral features that most strongly influence Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha are those at 0 and 9 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}, and many components were already required for our fiducial model in these features, particularly the former (5 components). We already discussed in Section 3.5 that no reasonable fit could be constructed without the very narrow ‘cold’ components in the 0 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} feature. However, removing a single broader component in the 0 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} feature, like that at −3-3 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}, results in a much higher AICC. The only velocity at which a new component could be added to these features was at 14 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} which produced a somewhat higher AICC (12.4) but very little change in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha (0.3 ppm). In the rest of the profile, a 0.4 ppm change in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha resulted from removing one of the two components in the sharp right-hand edge of the 75 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} feature. This feature is saturated in Mg ii and the two components in the fiducial fit were found to provide a marginally smaller AICC (by 0.4).

A.2 Central region

The structure of the most important spectral features for measuring Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha, at −237-237 and −140-140 to −120-120 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}, were thoroughly explored in this region. In the former, removing one of the reddest 3 components leaves a stable, statistically acceptable fit with an AICC ‘only’ 5 more than the fiducial fit. This fit leads to quite a large change in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha, 5 ppm, approximately the same as the statistical uncertainty in this region. While the AICC change of 5 is within our accepted AICC change threshold of 10, it is still regarded as ‘strong’ evidence against this model (Jeffreys, 1961). Nevertheless, we include it in our estimate for profile modelling systematic errors in this region. For the double feature between −140-140 and −120-120 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}, removing the component at −127-127 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} in Mg i/ii results in a lower AICC, but Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha only changes by 2 ppm. Although the feature at −179-179 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} is relatively broad and does not constrain Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha strongly, it is interesting that removing one of the two components at its centre resulted in an unstable fit, causing other surrounding components to be rejected by vpfit in some species.

A.3 Left region

Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha is mainly constrained by the features at −533-533, −495-495 and −470-470 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}, and the three between −420-420 and −380-380 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}. Table 4 shows that the velocity structure fitted to the strongest of these, at −533-533 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1}, seems to have little effect on Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha, while that fitted to the −495-495 and −390-390 km s−1\textrm{km\,s}^{-1} features is less well determined – shifts in Δ​α/α\Delta\alpha/\alpha of ≈\approx1.5–2 ppm are found for alternative models which have similar AICC values as the fiducial model. We found no alternative stable fits with more components than the fiducial model.
